_metadata.scope: Ancestor (above-item) interpretations for gbs333 built from item-level interpretation.json files; currently covers Liber 1 Prologus, Liber 1 Distinctio 37, Liber 2 Distinctio 44, Liber 3 Distinctiones 23–25, their libri, and the whole work (the latter four partial).

gbs333-aD60.summary: The prologue to Book I is Biel's abridgment of Ockham's prologue, examining the epistemic status of theology. After a preamble that states the aim of theology (a savoring, charity-increasing knowledge of God), names Ockham as principal guide, and outlines three inquiries (theology as knowledge, its unity through its subject, and its practical or speculative character), the twelve questions proceed in three groups. The first group (qq. 1–8) concerns theology as knowledge. Q. 1 lays the epistemological foundation: it defines the wayfarer, evident knowledge, and theological truth, and develops Ockham's theory of intuitive and abstractive cognition and of apprehension and judgment. It concludes that God by absolute power can make some theological truths evident to a wayfarer, but not those requiring intuitive vision of God. Q. 2 defines scientific knowledge and the knowable proposition, sets out the divine distinctions and the distinct and indistinct concepts of God, and concludes that every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is demonstrable, against Scotus's ordering of divine rationes. Qq. 3–6 are briefer logical questions on attributes and their subjects (real distinctness, demonstrability of attributes of first subjects, definition as middle term, per se modes), carrying an Ockhamist semantics of abstract and connotative terms. Q. 7 concludes that theology as acquired under the common law is not science properly so called: its principles are believed, all theological habits except faith are open to an unbeliever, and the subalternation analogy fails. Q. 8 holds that acquired theology is an aggregate of specifically distinct habits, individuated by acts, while infused faith is one habit. The second group (q. 9) rejects Scotus's account of the subject of a science as virtually containing all its truths: the subject of a science is simply the subject of its conclusions, so theology has many subjects, of which God, Christ, or 'things and signs' may each be called first under different orders of primacy. The third group (qq. 10–12) treats praxis and practical knowledge. Praxis is any operation in the will's power, primarily acts of will, and is not really distinct from speculation. Practical and speculative knowledge are properly distinguished by their objects (conclusions directive of free action or not), with prudence differing from moral science as experience from doctrine. Theology contains both simply practical and simply speculative knowledge. Throughout, Biel follows Ockham against Scotus and Aquinas, engages Pierre d'Ailly and Gregory of Rimini, and stresses divine absolute power, ontological parsimony, and the limits of the wayfarer's knowledge of God.
claims: Theology as possessed by wayfarers under the common law is not science properly so called, because its principles are believed rather than evident, though God could by absolute power make some theological truths evident.
Contingent theological truths whose evidence requires intuitive vision of God cannot be made evident to a wayfarer; in this life we have only indistinct (common or composite) concepts of God.
Every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is in principle demonstrable.
Acquired theology is an aggregate of many specifically distinct habits rather than one habit; infused faith is one habit.
The subject of a science is just the subject of its conclusions; theology therefore has many subjects, and Scotus's virtual-containment account is rejected.

Praxis is any act in the will's power and is not really distinct from speculation; theology contains both practical and speculative knowledge, distinguished by whether its conclusions direct free action.
concepts: distinct vs. indistinct concepts of God

gbs333-aD2349.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I treats God's presence in creatures. The preamble summarizes Lombard's text in three conclusions: God is in all things by essence, presence, and power, more excellently in the saints by the grace of adoption, and most excellently in Christ by the grace of union. He is everywhere without change, circumscription, or limitation. And he remains in himself non-local and atemporal, independent of creation. The single question then examines the general mode of this presence: whether being everywhere and in all things through essence, presence, and power is proper to God alone. After distinguishing the modes of being-in (by power, presence, and essence) and of being in place (circumscriptive, definitive, repletive), Biel establishes that God is in all things through power, presence, and essence, and in every place repletively rather than locally. Following Ockham and Scotus against the inference attributed to Aquinas, he denies that God's immediate causality over all things by itself entails his essential omnipresence. He also distinguishes a contingent sense of universal presence, in principle communicable to a creature, from the necessary sense proper to God alone, a conditional necessity by which God cannot exist without being in whatever exists.
claims: God is present in all things by essence, presence, and power, with special and singular grades of indwelling in the saints and in Christ.
God is in every place repletively, without change, circumscription, or local motion, while remaining in himself non-local and atemporal.
God's immediate causal power over all things does not by itself entail his essential omnipresence (with Ockham and Scotus, against the Thomist inference).
Universal presence is proper to God alone only in a necessary, conditional sense; in a contingent sense it could be communicated to a creature.
concepts: repletive vs. circumscriptive and definitive presence

gbs333-d1e5684.summary: Distinction 44, the final distinction of Book II, turns from the causes and nature of sin (treated in the preceding distinctions) to the power to sin itself and its origin. The preamble summarizes Lombard's text in three conclusions: all power to act well or badly is from God; legitimately exercised power must be obeyed while its abuse is to be resisted; and when an inferior power commands against a superior, the superior is to be heeded. The question asks whether the power to sin was granted by God to the rational creature. Biel holds that the power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom. It evidences freedom but does not belong to its essence, since God and the confirmed blessed are free without it. It was therefore conferred by God and is in itself good, though not an unqualified perfection. Against objections drawn from Bonaventure, he insists that the power to sin, as an absolute reality, is simply from God, and that only the privative disorder of sin is not. The objections are answered by distinctions between God's will of good pleasure and his preceptive will, and between positive powers and mere failings, and by arguing that freedom, the power to sin itself, assimilates man to the supremely free God. The distinction, and with it Biel's commentary on Book II, closes with a doxology and explicit.
claims: All power to act well or badly is from God; legitimate power is to be obeyed and its abuse resisted, with superior authority prevailing over inferior.
The power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom, was given by God, and is good in itself, though not a perfectio simpliciter.
Only the privative disorder of sin, not any positive reality in it, is not from God.
Freedom, including the power to sin, assimilates the rational creature to God, and its perfection lies in free conformity to the divine will.
concepts: obedience and resistance to abuse of power

gbs333-aD56.summary: Partial summary of Book I, resting only on the Prologue and Distinction 37 (2 of the book's 49 direct divisions have interpretations; Distinctions 1–36 and 38–48 are not covered). From these two parts, Book I appears as Biel's Ockhamist treatment of God and of theological knowledge of God. The Prologue establishes the epistemic framework. Theology as possessed by wayfarers is not strictly a science, since its principles are believed, though God could by absolute power make some theological truths evident. Our concepts of God in this life are only indistinct, common or composite. Acquired theology is an aggregate of habits with many subjects. It includes both practical and speculative knowledge, distinguished by whether its conclusions direct free action. Distinction 37 applies this framework to the divine presence: God is in all things by essence, presence, and power, repletively and without change, with special and singular indwelling in the saints and in Christ. Following Ockham and Scotus against Aquinas, Biel denies that causal immediacy alone entails essential omnipresence, and he treats universal presence as proper to God only in a conditional, necessary sense. Nothing should be inferred from this summary about the uncovered distinctions, which per the plan Biel gives at the opening of Distinction 1 cover the Trinity in itself (dd. 2–34) and the divine attributes of knowledge, power, and will (dd. 35–48).
claims: (Partial, from the Prologue) Theology in via is not science properly so called, and our knowledge of God is limited to indistinct concepts.
(Partial, from d. 37) God is present in all things by essence, presence, and power, and his causal immediacy does not by itself entail essential omnipresence.

gbs333-d1e4057.summary: Partial summary of Book II, resting only on Distinction 44, the book's final distinction (1 of 44 direct divisions has an interpretation; Distinctions 1–43 are not covered). The covered material shows Book II ending with the power to sin and its origin, after the preceding distinctions (as the d. 44 preamble notes) treated the causes and nature of sin. Biel argues that all power, including the power to sin, is from God. The power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom, and so good in itself though not an unqualified perfection, while only sin's privative disorder is not from God. Freedom assimilates the rational creature to the supremely free God. The summary says nothing about the creation, angels, human nature, grace, and the other topics of the uncovered distinctions.
claims: (Partial, from d. 44) The power to sin is identical with free will, comes from God, and is good in itself; only the disorder of sin is not from God.

gbs333-d1e1388.summary: Distinction 23 opens Book III's treatment of the virtues, gifts, and precepts as perfections of Christ the head together with his members. Its praeambulum sets out Lombard's plan: faith in itself (d. 23), in its object (d. 24), and in its subject (d. 25), followed by hope (d. 26) and charity (d. 27). It condenses the distinction into three conclusions on faith's definition, its formation by charity, and its unity and priority. Biel then asks two questions. The first, a general question on virtue laying the foundation for what follows, concludes, closely following Ockham, that virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, not a power, passion, or act. Being virtuous belongs first to acts, and only the will's act elicited because right reason actually dictates it is intrinsically virtuous. All other acts and habits are virtuous only by extrinsic denomination. Habits are absolute qualities generated by acts and co-causing similar acts. They are found in executive, cognitive, and probably sensitive powers and in the will, and their inclinations explain non-imputable first motions. Virtue grows by degrees and is lost through contrary habits or disuse. The second question asks whether one infused faith is sufficient and necessary for believing all credibles. Biel defines faith generally as a certain and firm adhesive cognition of religious truth received by revelation, most certain though not evident. He argues that acquired faith, grounded in belief in the Church, is necessary for any act of belief, and that natural reason cannot prove infused faith necessary, though Scripture and the Church teach it. Infused faith is one for all articles, makes belief more perfect and firm, and is lost only through pertinacious error. Acquired faiths differ by article, and the same habit of faith can be successively formed and unformed by charity.
claims: Faith is treated in itself (d. 23), in its object (d. 24), and in its subject (d. 25).
Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, and only the will's elicited acts according to right reason are intrinsically virtuous.
Habits are absolute qualities generated by acts that co-cause similar acts, and virtue grows and decays by degrees.
Faith is a certain and firm adhesive cognition of religious truth received by revelation, most certain though not evident.
Acquired faith, resting on belief in the Church, is required for every act of belief; the necessity of infused faith is known by faith, not proved by reason.
Infused faith is one for all articles and is lost only through pertinacious error or doubt.
Charity forms faith by ordering its acts to God, so the same habit can be successively formed and unformed.

gbs333-d1e1528.summary: Distinction 24 turns from the substance of faith to its object, asking whether faith can concern things seen and known. Its praeambulum states Lombard's conclusions: proper faith concerns only what is not apparent. Peter saw the man Christ suffer but believed that the sufferer was God. Faith and understanding are mutually prior. Biel's single question asks whether faith and science of the same revealed truth can coexist in one soul. Science is cognition of a necessary conclusion demonstrated from evident principles. So, against Aquinas, wayfarers' theology is not science even if subalternated to the theology of the blessed, since a conclusion follows the weaker premise. Faith covers demonstrable necessary truths as well as contingent ones. Some credibles are knowable by wayfarers (God's existence), some only by the blessed (the Trinity, demonstrable from proper concepts of God), and contingent ones by neither. Infused faith can coexist with science and clear vision of the same object. Acquired faith cannot, because their acts, involving obscurity and evidence, are contrary. Scripture yields faith, not science, since it proceeds by revelation. Theological study yields opinion and some science and equips the theologian to defend the faith, but never makes purely credible truths scientifically known. The prophets had divinely caused certitude excluding all doubt. Miracles strengthen faith without making it evident. God can cause evident knowledge of articles in a wayfarer without the beatific vision. An article of faith is any revealed truth pertaining to religion, binding explicitly or implicitly.
claims: Faith properly concerns only what is not apparent or evidently known.
Wayfarers' theology is not a science, even if subalternated to the theology of the blessed.
Some credibles are scientifically knowable by wayfarers, some only by the blessed, and contingent ones by none.
Infused faith can coexist with science of the same truth; acquired faith cannot.
Scripture and preaching confirmed by miracles produce faith, not science or evidence.
God can cause evident knowledge of articles in wayfarers without the beatific vision.
concepts: abstractive and intuitive cognition of God

gbs333-d1e1584.summary: Distinction 25 treats faith in its subject, the believers. It asks what faith the fathers of both testaments had and what is required of the simple. Its praeambulum states that faith in the mediator was always necessary for salvation, though it grew over time in the number of explicit articles and in devotion. Learned and simple alike were bound to fuller faith, and faith and hope pass away in the homeland while charity remains. Biel's single question asks whether all the faithful must believe explicitly all the articles of the Apostles' Creed. He expounds the Creed's fourteen articles by content (or twelve by apostolic author) and the additional Nicene and Athanasian creeds. He then distinguishes explicit faith from implicit faith in a general proposition, above all in whatever the Church believes. Implicit faith excludes pertinacity and so protects against heresy and can even preserve merit in invincible error. Infused faith, and actual faith for adults, was necessary in every age. Infused faith is the same in both testaments, while acquired faith about the Redeemer differs by tense. Since the fall, general faith in a mediator has been necessary for all, more particular faith as revelation grew, and God aids whoever does what is in him. All must believe everything implicitly. Explicit faith is owed according to office and capacity: the greater must know what their teaching requires, while the simple must explicitly believe in God, his rewarding, the Redeemer, the Trinity in a general way, and the articles celebrated in the Church's feasts. All must avoid pertinacious error. The Creed suffices because all Scripture reduces to the article on the Church. The articles have not grown in number but in explication, devotion, and firmness. Pope and Church cannot create articles but only define existing Catholic truth. Reason removes merit when it compels assent but increases it when charity seeks to understand and defend the faith.
claims: Faith in the mediator was necessary for salvation in every age, with the required explicitness growing with revelation.
Implicit faith in whatever the Church believes protects against heresy, because it excludes pertinacity.
Infused faith is the same across the testaments, while acquired faith about the Redeemer differs with tense.
All must believe everything implicitly; explicit faith is required according to office and capacity.
The Apostles' Creed sufficiently contains all articles, since all Scripture reduces to the article on the Church.
Neither pope nor Church can create new articles; they define what was always Catholic truth.
Reason removes merit only when it is the compelling ground of assent.

gbs333-d1e54.summary: Partial summary of Book III, resting only on Distinctions 23–25, the treatment of faith (3 of the book's 40 direct divisions have interpretations; Distinctions 1–22 and 26–40 are not covered). According to the plan in the d. 23 preamble, distinctions 1–22 treat Christ the head alone. The following distinctions treat head and members together with respect to the perfections of virtues, gifts, and grace: theological virtues (faith dd. 23–25, hope d. 26, charity d. 27), cardinal virtues (d. 33), gifts of the Holy Spirit (d. 34), and precepts (from d. 37). In the covered distinctions, Biel first lays an Ockhamist foundation on virtue in general. Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, and only the will's elicited acts in accord with right reason are intrinsically virtuous. He then treats faith in itself, its object, and its subject. Faith is a certain, firm, non-evident adhesive cognition of revealed religious truth. Acquired faith, grounded in belief in the Church, is required for every act of belief, while infused faith, known only by faith, is one for all articles and lost by pertinacious error. Faith cannot coexist with demonstrative science of the same truth when acquired, though infused faith can. Wayfarers' theology is not science. Implicit faith in the Church's belief guards against heresy. The Apostles' Creed sufficiently contains all articles. Explicit faith is owed according to office and capacity, with faith in a mediator necessary in every age. The Church defines but does not create articles. Nothing here describes Biel's treatment of the incarnation, hope, charity, the cardinal virtues, the gifts, or the precepts in the uncovered distinctions.
claims: (Partial, from dd. 23–25) Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, intrinsically virtuous only in the will's elicited acts.

(Partial) Faith is a certain, firm, non-evident adhesive cognition of revealed truth; acquired faith grounded in the Church is necessary for belief, while infused faith is known by faith and is one for all articles.
(Partial) Wayfarers' theology is not science, and acquired faith cannot coexist with science of the same truth.
(Partial) Implicit faith in the Church guards against heresy, and explicit faith is owed according to office and capacity.
(Partial) The Church defines but cannot create articles of faith.

gbs333.summary: Partial summary of Gabriel Biel's Collectorium (Epitome and Collectorium on the four books of the Sentences), resting only on the partial summaries of Book I (Prologue and d. 37), Book II (d. 44), and Book III (dd. 23–25). Book IV has no interpretations (3 of 4 direct children covered, all themselves partial). As the Praeambulum states, the work abridges William of Ockham's Sentences teaching, supplemented where Ockham is silent by other doctors consistent with his principles, and follows Lombard's distinctions with a summary of Lombard's text before the questions. The covered portions show a consistently Ockhamist approach. Theology as wayfarers possess it is not science properly so called, a point Book III reinforces by arguing that acquired faith cannot coexist with demonstrative science of the same truth. God could by absolute power make some theological truths evident, and our concepts of God in this life are indistinct. God is present in all things by essence, presence, and power, though causal immediacy does not by itself entail that presence. Free will, identical with the power to sin, is God's good gift. Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, intrinsically present only in the will's elicited acts. Faith is a firm, certain, non-evident assent to revealed truth that rests on acquired faith in the Church, with infused faith a supernatural gift known by faith. Implicit faith in the Church's belief protects against heresy, and the Church defines but cannot create articles. These are samples; they do not represent the full scope of the four books.
claims: (Partial) The Collectorium is an epitome of Ockham's Sentences commentary, filled out with other doctors consistent with Ockham's principles.

(Partial) In the covered portions Biel holds that wayfarers' theology is not strictly a science, that God is omnipresent though not merely in virtue of causal immediacy, and that the power to sin, as free will, is from God.
(Partial) Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, intrinsically present only in the will's elicited acts.
(Partial) Faith rests on acquired faith in the Church's authority, supplemented by infused faith, and implicit faith in the Church guards against heresy.
